content.text:
Mostly healthy, but the `Plugins` section is a real bug, not just noise.

**What's fine**

- The `plugin repositories: [null]` / `looking up plugins:` / `already installed:` lines and the CLion `Installation home directory` + `Debug | ByteBufferAsyncProcessor …` block are the JetBrains launchers' own stdout. jbsync shells out to `<launcher> installPlugins <id>` and inherits stdio (`src/plugins.rs:624`), so that leaks through. Ugly, harmless.
- The five `no changes` blocks mean the settings sync itself is a clean no-op.

**What's wrong: the installs are never actually needed, and will repeat forever**

`org.toml.lang` is *bundled* in four of your five IDEs — I checked each `product-info.json`:

| IDE | `bundledPlugins` has `org.toml.lang` | planned |
|---|---|---|
| RustRover / CLion / IntelliJ IDEA / PyCharm | yes | yes ❌ |
| WebStorm | no (it's in the config `plugins/toml` dir) | no ✅ |

That's exactly the four IDEs in your `Plugins` section, and exactly why each launcher immediately answers `already installed`.

The cause is in `plan_installs` (`src/plugins.rs:588`): it skips a plugin only when it's in the IDE's *config* `plugins/` directory (`installed(ide, true)` reads `<config>/plugins`, `src/plugins.rs:268`). Bundled plugins live in the app bundle, so they never show up there. jbsync does know about them — `bundled_ids` reads `bundled_plugins` from `product-info.json` (`src/plugins.rs:250`) — but that set only feeds `capabilities()` for dependency resolution; it's never consulted for the skip. So `capable` contains `org.toml.lang`, the verdict comes back compatible, and an install is planned anyway.

Consequences, each run:
- Four IDE CLI processes launched to do nothing (that's also where the CLion debug spew comes from).
- The summary claims work that isn't work — it will print those four lines on every sync, indefinitely. Nothing converges.

Side note on why it entered the manifest at all: `collect()` uses `installed(ide, false)`, which excludes bundled, so WebStorm's hand-installed TOML copy got published to `plugins.json`; every bundled-TOML IDE then looks "missing" to the planner.

**Fix** — one line in `plan_installs`, skip anything the IDE can already satisfy:

```rust
if present.contains_key(&plugin.id) || capable.contains(&plugin.id) {
    continue;
}
```

`capable` is already computed at `src/plugins.rs:581`. Note ordering: `capabilities()` applies `plugins.capability` remove rules, so a user who explicitly removed an id would still get an install planned — which is the right behavior.

Want me to apply that and add a regression test (bundled plugin present in `product-info.json` ⇒ no install action)? Separately, worth considering capturing the launcher's stdout instead of inheriting it, so only failures print.

### Why Git is a subprocess

jbsync runs the `git` binary rather than linking a Git library. That keeps
authentication as whatever already works for you — SSH agent, Keychain, Windows
Credential Manager, `gh auth`, hardware keys — instead of reimplementing it, and
avoids a C dependency in every one of eight release targets.

When another machine has published since this one last looked, jbsync merges
semantically and then records the remote as a parent, so history stays honest
without Git's line merge ever touching a settings file.

---

## 6. Plugins

jbsync records which third-party plugins you have in `plugins.json`, with the
compatibility metadata from each descriptor. Other machines install them from
Marketplace through the IDE's own launcher.

**Plugin directories are never copied.** They contain compiled code and
sometimes native libraries; copying them between machines — let alone between
macOS and Windows — is unsound.

Compatibility is checked before anything is installed: build ranges (including
`.*` wildcards), required modules against what each IDE provides, and
`incompatible-with` declarations. A Python-only plugin is not offered to CLion.

`jbsync plugins` shows the manifest and the verdict per IDE. Installation is
opt-in via `jbsync sync --install-plugins`, because it launches the IDE binary
and that should not happen behind your back.

It also reports plugins that are **already installed but cannot load**, which is
a different question from what to install next. A plugin put there by hand — or
copied in by Toolbox while setting the IDE up — may declare a dependency the
product cannot satisfy:

```
Installed but cannot load:
  WebStorm2026.2: com.github.l34130.mise needs org.toml.lang
      fix: install org.toml.lang in WebStorm2026.2
```

That is the same failure the IDE reports at startup, found before you open it.

### `[[plugins.rule]]` — force a verdict

Overrides jbsync's compatibility check for one plugin. Useful when a plugin's
declared build range is stale but it works fine, or when a plugin belongs in
one product and nowhere else.

```toml
[[plugins.rule]]
id = "com.example.plugin"    # the plugin ID from its descriptor
ide = "*"                    # glob over IDE directory name / product; default "*"
action = "allow"             # "allow", "deny", or "only"
```

| `action` | Effect on IDEs matching `ide` | Effect on every other IDE |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allow` | install, whatever the compatibility check says | nothing — the rule is silent |
| `deny` | never install | nothing — the rule is silent |
| `only` | install, whatever the compatibility check says | never install |

`only` is the one action that speaks for IDEs it does not name, which is what
makes "this plugin belongs in CLion alone" a single rule:

```toml
# Zig development lives in CLion. Nothing else gets ZigBrains.
[[plugins.rule]]
id = "com.falsepattern.zigbrains"
ide = "CLion*"
action = "only"
```

Other IDEs then report the reason in `jbsync plugins` and in a sync:

```
WebStorm2026.2: skip com.falsepattern.zigbrains (only for CLion*)
```

Remember a plugin's **dependencies** need the same treatment, or they keep
installing everywhere on their own. ZigBrains pulls in LSP4IJ, so both are
confined together:

```toml
[[plugins.rule]]
id = "com.redhat.devtools.lsp4ij"
ide = "CLion*"
action = "only"
```

Writing these by hand is optional — `jbsync plugins only <id> --ide "CLion*"`
appends the block for you, leaving the rest of the file and its comments alone.
See [Keep a plugin in one IDE only](recipes.md#keep-a-plugin-in-one-ide-only).

**Precedence.** Rules are read top to bottom and the **last** one that matches
wins, so put general rules first and narrow exceptions after them. This is why
`only` is worth reaching for: the two-rule spelling of the same intent is a
blanket `deny` followed by a narrower `allow`, and in the other order it
silently does nothing.

```toml
# Equivalent to the single `only` rule above — and easy to get wrong.
[[plugins.rule]]
id = "com.falsepattern.zigbrains"
ide = "*"
action = "deny"

[[plugins.rule]]
id = "com.falsepattern.zigbrains"
ide = "CLion*"
action = "allow"
```

content.text:
Real bug, and a slightly embarrassing one for a settings store. Fixed and pushed as `423acf5`.

**What it was.** jbsync writes `.gitattributes` into every store (`src/backend/git.rs:27`), and it read:

```
* -text -diff=auto
```

The intent shows in the trailing `auto` — *let Git decide*. But a leading `-` **unsets** an attribute, so that says `diff` unset, and an unset `diff` means Git calls every path binary. A store whose entire content is XML and TOML was recording its history as "Binary files differ".

I confirmed it rather than reasoning about it, with three throwaway repos changing one line of a `.toml`:

| `.gitattributes` | Result |
|---|---|
| `* -text -diff=auto` | `Bin 22 -> 22 bytes` |
| `* -text` | `1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)` with the real diff |
| *(none)* | same real diff |

**Was the `-diff` load-bearing?** No. The stated purpose is byte-for-byte fidelity across platforms, and `-text` alone delivers it: with `core.autocrlf=true`, a CRLF file round-trips through commit and checkout with its bytes intact. That's now a test rather than a claim in a comment.

**The fix** is `* -text`, leaving `diff` unspecified so Git detects binary by looking for NUL bytes. Existing stores are migrated when the file matches the old text **exactly** — a hand-edited `.gitattributes` is someone's own decision and is left alone, which is also a test.

**Best part: the repair is retroactive.** Attributes are applied when a diff is generated, not when the commit was made. Your `5b25e5b` commit that showed `Bin 0 -> 488 bytes` now renders its real 18-line diff — your whole settings history becomes readable, not just future commits.

I applied the migration to your live store, so `~/.jbsync/data/.gitattributes` is now `* -text` and shows as modified. Your next `jbsync sync` commits it, and it reaches your other machines from there. Nothing else touched. Worth knowing: the released binary you have installed only writes that file when it's missing, so it won't undo this before you update.
